summary: Helps 6–7 year-olds separate an OBSERVATION (what you could see, measure, or record, that everyone would agree on) from an INTERPRETATION (your idea about why, which could be wrong or have alternatives). Core moves: label statements as observation or interpretation, catch tell-tale 'why' words ('because', 'so', 'wanted to', 'must have'), and rewrite a mixed statement back to only what was actually observed — while treating interpretation as valuable, not wrong. Holding data and explanation apart is intended as the foundation for later evidence-based reasoning, letting a learner change their mind with evidence or consider another explanation.
misconceptions: Reporting an interpretation as if it were an observation ('the plant was thirsty' rather than 'the plant drooped').
Thinking interpretation is 'wrong' or unscientific, rather than a separate, useful layer.
Believing there is only one possible interpretation of an observation.
Missing the interpretation smuggled in by a 'because' clause.
Assuming that because an interpretation feels obvious it must be the observation itself.
Treating a feeling attributed to an object ('the ice was sad') as an observation.

activities.title: Two Buckets: sort what I saw from what I think
steps: Watch or recall a vivid shared event, e.g. an ice cube in a sunny window slowly turning to a puddle.
Take statement cards one at a time and place each into a WHAT I SAW bin or a WHAT I THINK bin. Examples to sort: 'The ice got smaller', 'The ice was sad', 'It melted because the sun was warm'.
When sorting 'It melted because the sun was warm', notice the word 'because' — ask yourself: did I SEE the sun make it melt, or am I thinking that?
Say aloud why each 'saw' card is something everyone looking would agree on.

Discuss how the same observation ('the puddle got smaller') could have more than one explanation (the sun dried it, or the water soaked into the ground) — both of which are ideas about why, not things seen.
activities.insight: The puddle shrinking is something everyone would agree on; the 'because…' is a story I added, and my story might be wrong — so keeping it separate from what I saw is what lets me later test or change it.

activities.title: Snip the 'because' tail: rewrite to a pure observation
steps: Take a mixed sentence such as 'The ice melted because the sun was warm' or 'The sun dried up the puddle'.
Cross out or remove the interpretation part so only what was actually observed remains (e.g. 'The ice melted' / 'The puddle got smaller').
Read the trimmed sentence back and check that everyone watching would agree it is what happened.
Then, separately, state your interpretation starting with 'I think…' so both layers are named and kept apart.
activities.insight: Stripping a statement back to the observation is an active move that shows which part was the evidence and which part was my explanation added on top.

activities.title: Science-buddy dialogue: 'What did you SEE? What do you THINK it means?'
steps: Look at a shared picture or scene (melting snowman, wilting plant, rolling ball).
Answer two separate questions in turn: first 'What did you actually SEE?', then 'What do you THINK that means?'
Notice and name any time an idea slips into the 'saw' answer, and move it to the 'think' answer.
Offer a second possible explanation for the same thing you saw.
activities.insight: A single moment splits into two things — the seen fact and my idea about why — and one observation can support more than one 'why'.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap scene: observation first, idea underneath
steps: Explore a single scene (melting snowman, wilting plant) by tapping or looking at marked spots.
At each spot, first read the 'Observation: …' (what can be seen), then lift a flap to reveal 'and what might that mean?' with a candidate interpretation.
Say back, in your own words, which part was the observation and which was the idea about why.
activities.insight: Every noticed fact can have an interpretation layered on top; seeing the two-layer structure modelled is intended to make the pattern memorable.

activities.title: Check: observation or interpretation?
steps: Given short vivid statements, label each as an observation or an interpretation. Include tempting mixed statements as the hard cases.
Complete sentence frames: 'I observed …' with a pure observation, and 'I think …' with the matching interpretation.
Explain for one item how you can tell which is which.
activities.insight: I can reliably tell a seen fact from an idea about why, including in tricky mixed wording.

checkQuestion: Look at three things a child wrote after watching a puddle outside: 'The puddle got smaller.' 'The sun dried up the puddle.' 'The puddle was shrinking.' Which of these are things you could actually SEE happening, and which is a guess about WHY? How can you tell the difference?
checkAnswer: 'The puddle got smaller' and 'the puddle was shrinking' are observations — things you could actually see. 'The sun dried up the puddle' is an interpretation — a guess about the cause you can't see directly (you see the puddle shrink, not the sun doing it). A strong response separates what was seen from the explanation of why, and notes that the interpretation could be wrong even when the observation is right — maybe the water soaked into the ground.
